analysis.one_liner: Directs OSHA to create federal rules protecting workers from dangerous heat on the job.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after introduction it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which took no action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Labor to write a federal rule protecting workers from extreme heat. Employers in hot workplaces — farms, construction sites, warehouses, kitchens — would have to provide drinking water, paid rest breaks in shade or air conditioning, training, emergency response plans, and could not punish workers who report heat dangers. The bill sat in the Senate labor committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly tens of millions of outdoor and indoor workers exposed to dangerous heat — farmworkers, construction crews, warehouse and delivery workers, kitchen and laundry staff — gain enforceable rights to water, paid shade breaks, training, and protection from retaliation. Heat deaths and illnesses fall, and the bill's own findings note those harms fall disproportionately on Black and Brown workers [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Outdoor and indoor workers in hot jobs

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Department of Labor to issue a binding federal standard requiring employers to protect workers from excessive heat, both outdoors and in hot indoor workplaces.
Requires employers to provide water, scheduled and paid rest breaks in shaded or climate-controlled spaces, acclimatization plans for new workers, and emergency medical response plans.
Requires annual training for workers and supervisors, written heat prevention plans in the language workers understand, and heat illness and death recordkeeping.
Protects workers from employer retaliation for reporting heat hazards, and pays piece-rate workers for required heat-related rest breaks.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in heat-exposed industries — agriculture, construction, warehousing, food processing — bear the cost of water, shade or cooling, paid rest breaks, training, heat plans, and recordkeeping [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose real compliance costs on employers — paid rest breaks, cooling equipment, air conditioning or shade, annual training, written plans, and recordkeeping — which fall hardest on small farms and contractors operating on thin margins.

To move quickly, the bill allows an interim final standard that bypasses some normal rulemaking procedures (including ordinary notice-and-comment requirements under the Administrative Procedure Act), which reduces the usual opportunity for employers and the public to shape the rules before they take effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: a federal heat standard would prevent thousands of heat-related illnesses and deaths among farmworkers, construction workers, warehouse workers, and others, with employers bearing the cost of water, shade or cool space, paid breaks, and training — costs that are real but modest relative to the harm, and partly offset by lower turnover and productivity losses. The main legitimate objections are compliance cost for small employers in hot climates and the bill's use of an expedited interim standard that skips some normal rulemaking steps. Set against 815 recorded worker heat deaths in 25 years, the bill's design is sound.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 12, 2021, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the Senate floor, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with no vote.
It had 17 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican support in the Senate.
The bill's findings document the stakes: 815 US workers died from heat between 1992 and 2017, nearly 70,000 were seriously injured, and the numbers are considered undercounts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in hot industries — farms, construction sites, and warehouses — kept operating without federal heat-safety rules, avoiding the cost of breaks, shade, and cooling.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers in hot industries, farm to warehouse

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push for a federal OSHA heat standard.

for.name: 16 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Padilla, Merkley, Warren, Cortez Masto, and Baldwin as original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, and the HELP Committee's Republican members had the votes to keep it from advancing out of committee.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 12, 2021 and took no action — no markup, no vote, no report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents; no Senate Republican signed on, and the Republican-majority opposition on the HELP Committee was enough to keep the bill from advancing.

industries.note: Farm work has the highest heat illness rates; the bill would require paid shade breaks, water, acclimatization plans, and compensation for piece-rate workers during rest breaks, cutting into harvest output and labor control.
Outdoor construction would face mandated rest breaks, hydration, exposure monitoring, and heat plans, adding cost and slowing work schedules on hot days.

industries.industry: Warehousing and hot indoor workplaces (bakeries, kitchens, laundries, steel mills)
industries.note: Indoor hot workplaces would need cooling, ventilation, monitoring, and training, costs the bill shifts from workers' bodies onto employers.
